title: Agenda: Matthew and Cyrus, Wednesday 2026-10-21
sub: The topics Matthew brings to his meeting with Cyrus on Wednesday 2026-10-21. Most are Cyrus's own questions from their meeting on Friday 2026-10-16. A work in progress: compiled over the two days before the meeting and updated as items move, so each item says where it stands, as of when, and what it needs from the meeting.
short: #2635's CI is green: every failure fixed. The three causes ^report(18) found are fixed, one of them a real bug in incremental statics; with #2699 merged, Fast checks and Full tests both pass, for the first time since 2026-10-01.
Cyrus's two tiles asks: what is missing is selection, not tiles. The explainer's examples and the livelit model views are already tiles; only the revealed model can be selected (^report(19)).
Long types in Γ: a draft PR, #2698, stacked on #2676 (the cursor inspector's long types).
The performance PRs' correctness: an argument for each of the 19, in a report to come, with more correctness tests. The corners and weak hashes it found are fixed on their branches.
The merge plan for dev: which PRs are first, and how the livelits PRs meet #2469 once it lands.

items.title: #2635's CI: why it failed, and a fix for every failure
items.body:
^report(18) found three causes, all from merging #2469 (modular editors) into the livelits branch, with neither branch broken on its own: 8 DefStaticsParity module cases (modules analyzed whole since the merge), one typed-table test (Editing.TableDecorations 1, from dev's canonical completion, #2374), and one mismatch in the slide corpus. As of 2026-10-19 each has a fix:

  • the table test's input, so that its hidden error still comes from table syntax (27f100e37c);
  • the corpus mismatch, a real bug in incremental statics: a livelit use was not analyzed again when the livelit it applies changed, so after an edit it kept its old expansion (1131a457e4);
  • the 8 module cases, by #2699, which brings Andrew Blinn's per-member module analysis on Modules II (a6b5478f52, from #2687) into #2635, with one fix of its own: a livelit definition is no longer analyzed as a module (223357135a).

On GitHub, #2699 passed Fast checks and Full tests and was merged into #2635 (90ed4505bf): #2635's Fast checks now pass, the first time since the branch was made on 2026-10-01; its Full tests passed too (1 h 32 min, done 15:06), so #2635 is green on 90ed4505bf. At 15:10 one more commit went on top, a full-screen button for a livelit's picture (5961401df2), and its checks passed too (Fast checks and Full tests on 5961401df2, by 16:30). #2635's conflicts with its base are resolved too (cf325d4f61). The whole story, with today's update, is ^report(18).

What happened after it, step by step: ^report(18)'s five next steps, two done, two partly and one for this meeting, and what is still open (#2597's table test, a conflict in one file again since #2597 moved, the merge plan): ^report(23).

Since, 2026-10-20: both livelits PRs are up to date with dev and mergeable. #2597 merged dev (dev's segmented loader, settings panel, ascriptions, the clipboard shim's removal) and is green on its own branch, Fast checks and Full tests (6fbc8268fc); #2635 merged dev and the new #2597 and is green the same way (d14229ee66). Both have since taken the fix for item 5 (2cf1b59c37; #2635's merge 3d7d5baca0), #2597 green on Fast checks. One risk found on the way: #2635's quick suite took 11.5, 18 and then over 20 minutes on three runs, against the step's 20-minute limit, and the last stopped there with no test failing (#2597's takes about 5); a rerun is going.
items.meeting: Confirm both PRs are green. Whether the quick suite's 20-minute limit should rise, or #2635's slowest suites move to Full tests. The corpus bug is the kind the correctness items below are about: the parity tests caught it.

items.title: Livelits' model views as read-only tiles, with the tiles' selection UX
items.body: ^report(19): a livelit's model, revealed with its eye, is the one view outside the editor that already has read-only tiles with a caret, Shift+Arrow selection, the inspector and the right-click menu. Two gaps, seen on #2635: a mouse drag over the model selects by character, not by tile (its ends do not snap to tiles, as they do in the editor); and while the revealed model has focus, the rest of the editor draws blank until the eye closes. A livelit's head and params lines are HTML inputs, by design.
items.meeting: Is the revealed model's read-only selection what Cyrus wants on every look-only view? ^report(19) suggests one shared read-only, selectable view for all 16 of them.

items.title: The explainer's examples as read-only tiles
items.body: ^report(19): the examples are already tiles, in a locked cell editor. They take focus but no caret, no selection and no menu. The inline code in the explanations is plain text. So, as with the model views, the ask comes down to selection and the menu.
items.meeting: The same question; and should the inline code become tiles too?

items.title: Long types in Γ, laid out as the result type is
items.body:
#2698 (a draft, stacked on #2676, which does the same for the cursor inspector): a toggle on each entry in Γ lays a long type, or an alias's definition, out under its name in at most 60 columns, and Γ grows to 40% of the window while one is open. On the tutorial, the toggle appears on the 147 of 249 entries that are cut off. Later steps: unfold all, unfold the caret's variable by itself, and module members one per line.

A related bug (^ticket(396)): opening Γ on #2635's Scenes slide freezes the browser. A lead: even on a 4-line program Γ draws 6,802 tokens, because the context holds the prelude's types (ColorScheme, ColorRoles, …) and each is printed whole as tiles.
items.meeting: Review #2676, then #2698? Which of the later steps matter?

items.title: Why expanding Html said it was not found
items.body: Why: Html is a module, not a type. The HTML type is its member Html.T, where the old global alias HTML lives now. The way to ask the full view what a type is, type X = Html in ..., names Html as a type, which it is not; the inspector said only "Html not found" (and "HTML not found" for the old name). type X = Html.T in ... was fine. Reproduced on GitHub: type X = Html in 1 and type X = HTML in 1 each mark the name as a free type variable. Fixed on #2597 (2cf1b59c37; #2635 next): the inspector now says "Html is a module, not a type; its types: Html.T, Html.App", and for an old alias "HTML not found: it is Html.T now"; the full view of type X = Html.T in also shows what Html.T is. Four tests.
items.meeting: Whether the message is enough, or a module's name should also work where a type is expected (meaning its T).

items.title: Do the performance PRs keep typing and evaluation correct?
items.body:
Cyrus asked for more analysis and coverage of functional correctness. For each PR against #2609 (the performance tracking issue), a report will argue why it computes the same types and values as before: what it caches, skips or shares, the key it is looked up by, what invalidates it, and what it assumes. Any PR whose argument does not hold is called out. And more correctness tests: a new PR to dev, and tests on each PR.

One such check exists already: the DefStaticsParity tests compare incremental statics with a cold analysis and with monolithic statics after each edit. They caught the livelit bug fixed on 2026-10-19 (the first item).

Drafted on 2026-10-19: the report, ^report(21), with an argument for each of the 19 PRs; it goes up after Matthew has read it. The tests are a ticket of their own.

The tests, as a draft PR to dev: #2700 turns the incremental-against-fresh property back on for programs that evaluate to a value, adds six recursive-let cases, and compares incremental with fresh evaluation after 150 literal edits across the 73 corpus programs. Checked against a deliberately broken reuse check: the recursive cases and the corpus test catch it; the random property alone does not.

Fixed on their branches, 2026-10-19: the two PRs the report found changing a result in a corner, both confirmed by running. #2610's load fallback no longer turns x - y into x ¿ - y when it splits a long program just after an operand: the joined pieces are remolded once, with three split tests. #2651 again reports the error for a module definition that names its own module (module F = fun x -> F(x)), and keeps, with a test, its other change: a module under a one-member signature now evaluates to the module itself.

Hashes strengthened, 2026-10-19. Three PRs treat a structural hash as equality, so a collision would give a wrong answer, and two of those hashes let some collisions happen more easily than chance: a difference in one high bit of a part cancelled a second such difference. #2673's term hash now runs a finalizer per lane after every step (9de7d81838), and #2661's type hash, which #2681 uses too, has three such lanes, about 90 bits (67f676852b). Each comes with a test that flips every bit in every two of three parts. #2673 also gets a test pinning the two corners where its one walk decides differently from the old check, both safe (e1edf94a12), and #2675's description now names its one visible change: an outer binding that a recursive let shadows is flagged unused, which is right (confirmed with hazel analyze -W). #2610's fix passed its CI, and so did the three hash commits (#2661, #2673, #2681: Fast checks and Full tests).
items.meeting: Is an argument per PR, plus the tests, what Cyrus had in mind? Which PRs first?

items.title: Guarding correctness in CI, as the performance work caches more
items.body:
What guards results today, and what would guard the caches and reuse the performance PRs add (#2609). Today: DefStaticsParity checks that statics redone per definition agree with statics from scratch; the performance budgets (#2678) check cost, not results; and #2700 (a draft, green) turns the incremental-against-fresh property back on for evaluation results and adds Evaluator.IncrCorpus: 150 literal edits over the 73 corpus programs, each incremental result checked against evaluation from scratch. It was checked by mutation: with the reuse check made to ignore changed dependencies, it fails.

Proposed, in this order:

  1. Every cache has an off switch, and CI compares on against off. One differential harness over the slide corpus: types, marks, elaborations (ids aside), values, probes and test results, after random edits and from scratch, with each cache on and off. A performance PR registers its switch and gets the check. #2700's corpus test is its first case.
  2. The guards are tested too. For each cache, a deliberately wrong variant (a dependency ignored, a hash made to collide) must make the suite fail; run weekly, beside the extended tests. A guard that cannot fail guards nothing.
  3. Hash keys are checked for soundness. Equal hash implies equal term, for the type hash (#2661, #2681) and the term hash (#2673), with a census over the corpus.
  4. Every load path gives the same program. The fast loader, the recovering parser (#2610's segmented one), a saved slide's round trip and typing. ^report(21) found #2610's fallback turning x - y into x ¿ -y; ^ticket(472) is checking a saved Scenes slide whose livelit uses came back broken.
  5. The stack is tested merged. ^report(18)'s regressions came from merging two branches each green alone (#2469 into the livelits branch). A scheduled job that merges dev, #2469, #2597 and the performance PRs and runs both suites would find those before anyone merges.
  6. The checks are required (the item on gating dev, below): Fast checks required for dev, after quarantining Evaluator.Properties.
  7. Each performance PR says what it caches, as ^report(21) writes each one up: the key, what invalidates it, what it assumes, and the test that fails if the invalidation is wrong.
items.meeting: Which of these Cyrus wants, in which order, and which should become required checks; and whether #2700 comes out of draft first.

items.title: The merge plan for dev
items.body:
Cyrus's plan, broadly: first the PRs that have been waiting, then Andrew's modular editors (#2469, with the standard library, #2687), then the livelits and performance PRs, in some order. The livelits work is #2597 (the full livelits branch) and #2635 (livelits × modular editors, which merges #2469 into it). Most of the performance PRs are against dev already.

Merged into dev on 2026-10-19: #2679 (an ascription pushed through a value gives the value back), the first of the performance PRs to land.
items.meeting: Which PRs are the ones that have been waiting? Once #2469 lands, do the livelits PRs meet it through #2635, or by #2597 merging dev? And the order of the performance PRs.

items.title: Require the test jobs for merging into dev
items.body: dev is protected but requires no status check, so a red CI run, or a broken performance budget (#2678), is a signal, not a gate. A proposal for the maintainers: require the Fast checks job (10 to 15 minutes: the quick suite and the budgets), keep Full tests informational or require it too, and first quarantine the tests that fail by chance (Evaluator.Properties).

items.title: Undo: what it should restore, and what keeping it costs
items.body: Continuing the undo discussion. ^report(14) measured a tab on #2597 while one slider on the Full Body slide was moved again and again: it kept about 92 MB more after every edit and did not level off, and what it kept was the undo history, holding whole versions of the editor's state (types and statics, hashes of values, terms, layout), one per edit. Its plots follow four builds over twelve edits: #2597 as built (+1,048 MB after edit 12), the history capped at two states (levels off near +290 MB), the compaction from #2469 ported (near +160 MB), and #2635, which has the compaction (+52 MB).
items.meeting: What an undo should bring back, and so what each entry has to keep; and how far back, at what memory cost (the plots in ^report(14)).

items.title: Hazel tiles for a game's logic: Messed Up Dress Up as a Scratch-like world
items.body:
An idea, partly Matthew's to shape. Livelits show Hazel can express a great deal, but not yet fast enough to be a game's engine or its drawing. The game's logic is another matter, especially simple event declarations: when this happens in the game, queue that action, perhaps at once. Hazel tiles inside Messed Up Dress Up, customizing its behavior over its world, people and objects, would make each drive the other: more play, and more research. Such rules are small and run seldom next to the game's frames, so they fit Hazel's evaluator as it is.

Against Languages of Play (Martens and Hammer, 2017; HTML). The paper treats each game's interface as a programming language of player intent: its syntax the intents the game recognizes, its operational semantics the mechanics as inference rules for a step from a state and an intent to a new state and a response, its type system a contextual interface in which only what makes sense in the current state can be said; play traces are straight-line programs, and player skills general ones, with branching on the game's response, parameters typed by the resources they need, repetition and parallel composition, which it offers as a scripting language for modding and co-creative play.

  • Where they meet: "when this happens, queue that" is the paper's skill as a program, made reactive: a rule fires on a game event rather than being issued by the player, and its body is the same shape as the paper's do-then-case-on-the-response.
  • Where the paper goes further, and Hazel could follow: Dress Up's intents (walk, climb, sit, open, pull a lever, dress) as a typed syntax; the context (where the friend is, what is near) as the rules' type system, so a rule that can never apply is a type error rather than a silent no-op; the mechanics as inference rules, which Hazel can already hold as derivations, with the paper's "never gets stuck" as a property checked where the rules are written; play traces as structured values to query, as Hazel's probes already are.
  • What Hazel adds that the paper only anticipates (it cites Hazelnut): rules that are meaningful while half-written, with holes; the game's own controls inside a rule, as livelits (a slider for a jump's height, a picker for a place); and proof beside program in one editor.
  • Steps, smallest first: the events and intents as a Hazel sum type; rules as Hazel values the game reads into its queue; the context as types; traces the game logs as values Hazel can query; later, mechanics as inference rules.

Measured (^ticket(402), on #2635's code, the test build under node on a GitHub runner): a lever pulled flips every trapdoor a table of lever-to-trapdoor links names, written in plain Hazel, and again monadic (the rule returns commands as data, which a game would interpret against its globals, as Matthew asks: "we need global variables for simple games --- most scripts use them"). Statics and elaboration, once: 8 to 70 ms. Per pull: 0.7 ms with 10 links (0.95 ms monadic), 5.7 ms with 100, 65 ms with 1,000: linear in the table, since a list is scanned each pull. A trap room is a few links, so a twentieth of a 60-frames-a-second frame; drawing is what Hazel cannot do in time yet. The monad itself, $GameUpdate, with variables named by Fumola-like symbols, is ^ticket(479).

Sketched (^ticket(479)): the trap room's lever as a $GameUpdate program, a monad beside livelits' $UpdateCmd, its commands run by the game and each awaited (a walk takes time; the program resumes after), the game's variables named by typed, Fumola-like symbols:

# $GameUpdate: commands the game runs, each awaited, with do as for $UpdateCmd
#   pure(a)          | get(@sym) / set(@sym, v)  the game's variables, by symbol
#   walk_to(@thing)  | anim(name, ms) | wait(ms) | emit(event)  queued, e.g. Fell(pit)
# A symbol is a pointer into the game's saved state, typed by what it holds:
#   @room.lever(L) : Sym(Bool), @room.wiring : Sym(Wiring), @access.lever_far : Sym(Bool)

let pull_room_lever = fun side : Side ->
  do far <- get(@access.lever_far) in
  do _ <- (if far then pure(()) else walk_to(@room.lever_thing(side))) in
  do up <- get(@room.lever(side)) in
  do _ <- set(@room.lever(side), !up) in
  do _ <- anim("lever-turn", 1400) in
  do wiring <- get(@room.wiring) in             # normal, reversed or random
  do opened <- swing_pits(pits_worked(wiring, side)) in
  do at <- get(@friend.place) in
  if over_any(at, opened) then emit(Fell(at)) else pure(())
in

In the game today that is about 150 lines of JavaScript (the room's levers, its boulder levers, the placed levers' links, the walk to a lever and the pull, the pits' wiring). In Hazel, by estimate: the rules 60 to 90 lines; the monad's declaration in the builtins, as $UpdateCmd's is, 40; and in the game a command interpreter, about 100 lines of JavaScript, which keeps every animation and walk where it is now. Per pull, ~1 ms of Hazel (as measured above), the animations' time aside. What is new to Hazel: commands that suspend for the game, and symbols as typed pointers into a store Hazel does not own.
items.meeting: Whether this is worth a direction; which of the paper's layers to show first (typed intents and contextual types look nearest); and what is Matthew's to decide: which events and actions first, where the tiles sit in Dress Up, and who writes rules (M and N among them).

if_time: Livelit views evaluated in the worker (option B of ^report(5); ^ticket(18)): prototyped on #2635's branch (a view that takes 8 ms or more runs in the worker), not yet measured in a browser.
Three ports offered to #2469, with ^report(13)'s numbers (^ticket(54); offered on #2469 on 2026-10-19).
method: Started 2026-10-19 from the meeting's ticket on the work dashboard (^ticket(389)), which collects the topics as they come in; Matthew adds topics through Wednesday.
Each item gives who asked, its status and the time that status is from. PRs are hazelgrove/hazel's; commits are on the PR named beside them.

Each item has a copy item chip (^ticket(475)): it copies the item's number, its id (which stays when items are reordered), its title and its link. Pasted to Claude with a request (move it up or down, work on it now, to be readier to discuss it), it names the item exactly; the agenda is changed and republished in that turn.
